prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item also shows your previous context and question. Readers who knew what the team decided found that this version steers toward one particular resolution: it states or implies it, mentions elements that only one resolution would use, or frames the question so that one resolution is the obvious answer. You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

=== key a9c12f7fdb11
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Moment matching minimizes the KL divergence but leaves the choice of transformation ambiguous (e.g. for the Gamma, exp vs square, or an interpolation of them)
Write-up text before the decision: eft but they are still not perfect. The red line in the case of the Beta distribution, for example, goes to zero on the edges, where the originals go to infinity. [...] Laplace Matching is the process of finding the “right” transformation, e.g. it is on the correct domain, fast and as high-quality as possible. After the transformation has been found we have to develop the map from the parameters of the distribution \(\theta\) to \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) of the Gaussian approximation. Usually, this is done by computing the Laplace approximation in the chosen basis and inverting it. In some cases, e.g. the Dirichlet, the inversion is impossible and we have to use approximations for the inverse map. There is no clear optimal way of choosing the transformation since different transformation optimize different goals. However, we could show that the KL-divergence between the Gaussian and the exponential family distribution is minimized by moment matching, i.e. when the expected sufficient statistics are as similar as possible. This theoretical result still leaves some room for interpretation because the moments will never match perfectly. In the case of the Gamma distribution, for example, the original sufficient statistics of \([\log(x), x]\) can be transformed via the exponential function to be \([x, \exp(x)]\) or via the square to be \([\log(x), x^2]\). Both of these share one sufficient statistic with the Gaussian which has \([x, x^2]\).
Previous context: A researcher showed that the KL divergence between a Gaussian approximation and an exponential-family distribution is minimized by moment matching—making the expected sufficient statistics as similar as possible. But moments never match perfectly, so the theoretical result does not pin down a unique transformation. For the Gamma distribution, transformations via the exponential or the square each share one sufficient statistic with the Gaussian, leaving a genuinely open choice.
Previous question: How should the team choose among transformations when moment matching leaves the choice ambiguous?

Motivated by the idea that biological brains are specialized and modular, they are designing a follow-up study.

=== key adfa3330cf48
Kind of decision: whether to continue or drop a line of work
Problem: Whether the Laplace Bridge for BNNs is worth further work or practical use
Write-up text before the decision: ## Update When I wrote this post, the paper was not published yet. Now, after multiple resubmissions it has been accepted to UAI2022. Since we changed some substantial parts of the paper during the resubmissions, I decided to rewrite and update this post. The original post was published on the 3rd of November 2020. ### My personal opinion The idea underlying the Laplace Bridge for BNNs is very clean–you take a slow part in a Bayesian Neural Network and replace it with a fast approximation. However, the longer I worked with the LB, the more I realized that the approximation just isn’t that good. It has some theoretical problems but more importantly it is very easy to create examples with bad approximation quality. We could fix some of these problems with correction terms but even then the approximation quality of the LB is bad for some relevant cases. Therefore, the main reasons to care about the LB are: a) when inference speed matters much more than accuracy, e.g. when you just need some uncertainty estimate very quickly. Since drawing samples has gotten quite faster, I think there is basically nearly no practical use-case for the LB. b) A thought provoking way to think about BNNs. Working with the LB mostly showed me that there are many ways to achieve predictive uncertainty and we have probably only scratched the surface. Unfortunately, the current publishing environment doesn’t allow me to write papers in which I can express my opinion as honest as here. But on my blog I can say whatever I want and I think it’s important for other researchers to get my honest view.
Previous context: A researcher who developed a fast approximation replacing a slow sampling step in Bayesian neural networks found through extended work that the approximation quality is often poor, with easy-to-construct failure cases that correction terms only partially fixed. Meanwhile, sampling had become much faster, narrowing the practical niche to cases where speed matters far more than accuracy. The work had nonetheless been accepted for publication after multiple resubmissions.
Previous question: Is this method worth further work or practical use, and how should the researcher position it?
